symbols.name: \bar p
symbols.def: The known treatment-budget fraction, fixed along the sequence.

symbols.name: \mathcal N_{\bar p}
symbols.def: The set \(\mathcal N_{\bar p}=\{k\in\mathbb N:k\ge2,\ 1\le\lfloor\bar p k\rfloor\le k-1\}\) of population sizes with a nondegenerate exact budget.

symbols.name: n
symbols.def: The number of experimental units, restricted to the admissible index set.

symbols.name: V_n
symbols.def: The labeled finite population.

symbols.name: m_n
symbols.def: For \(n\in\mathcal N_{\bar p}\), the integer \(m_n=\lfloor\bar p n\rfloor\), which satisfies \(1\le m_n\le n-1\).

symbols.name: \mathcal A_n
symbols.def: For \(n\in\mathcal N_{\bar p}\), the set of all binary treatment assignments.

symbols.name: \Omega_n
symbols.def: For \(n\in\mathcal N_{\bar p}\), the nonempty set \(\Omega_n=\{z\in\mathcal A_n:\sum_{i\in V_n}z_i=m_n\}\).

symbols.name: \mathbf 0_n
symbols.def: The assignment treating no unit.

symbols.name: \mathbf 1_n
symbols.def: The assignment treating every unit.

symbols.name: \mathcal E
symbols.space: finite nonempty sets of exposure-mapping sequences
symbols.def: An analyst-specified menu known before randomization, with cardinality fixed along the sequence.

symbols.name: G_n
symbols.def: The observed ambient graph. Candidate mappings need not be local in it. Once \(\mathcal E\) is fixed, it is ancillary to the unrestricted frontier; in graph-local subclasses it may define, constrain, or organize a menu \(\mathcal E(G_n)\).

symbols.name: e
symbols.def: A generic candidate mapping in the menu.

symbols.name: \mathcal X_{i,e,n}
symbols.def: The range of unit \(i\)'s exposure coordinate for candidate \(e\).

symbols.name: e_{i,n}
symbols.def: The unit-level coordinate of candidate \(e\), without a graph-locality restriction.

symbols.name: d_{e,n}
symbols.def: The finite number \(d_{e,n}=\sum_{i\in V_n}|\mathcal X_{i,e,n}|\).

symbols.name: h_{i,e,n}
symbols.def: A response coordinate for candidate \(e\).

symbols.name: y
symbols.def: The complete finite-population response schedule, fixed before assignment.

symbols.name: \mathcal Y_n(\mathcal E)
symbols.def: For \(n\in\mathcal N_{\bar p}\), the union of the bounded table classes measurable with respect to at least one candidate in \(\mathcal E\).

symbols.name: Z
symbols.def: The realized exact-budget treatment vector.

symbols.name: \Theta
symbols.def: A budget-feasible randomized experimental design for \(Z\).

symbols.name: \mathcal D_n(\bar p)
symbols.def: For \(n\in\mathcal N_{\bar p}\), all assignment laws supported on \(\Omega_n\).

symbols.name: Y^{\mathrm{obs}}
symbols.def: The vector with coordinate \(Y_i^{\mathrm{obs}}=y_i(Z)\).

symbols.name: \mathsf O_n
symbols.def: The observed pair \(\mathsf O_n=(Z,Y^{\mathrm{obs}})\).

symbols.name: \widehat\theta
symbols.def: An arbitrary measurable function of the observed experiment. It may read the fixed known objects \(G_n,\mathcal E,\bar p\), but fixed-graph readability does not change the unrestricted function class because that constant can be compiled into the rule.

symbols.name: \theta_n(y)
symbols.def: The total treatment effect \(\theta_n(y)=n^{-1}\sum_{i\in V_n}[y_i(\mathbf 1_n)-y_i(\mathbf 0_n)]\).

symbols.name: \operatorname{RMSE}_n(\Theta,\widehat\theta;y)
symbols.def: The quantity \(\{\mathbb E_{Z\sim\Theta}[(\widehat\theta(\mathsf O_n)-\theta_n(y))^2]\}^{1/2}\).

symbols.name: \mathcal S_n
symbols.def: The finite set of sign-valued observed outcome vectors.

symbols.name: \mathcal B_n(\mathcal E)
symbols.def: The pairs \(\alpha=(e,b)\) with \(e\in\mathcal E\) and one sign \(b_{i,x}\in\{-1,1\}\) for every exposure-response coordinate.

symbols.name: \alpha
symbols.def: A candidate mapping together with a sign at each of its response coordinates.

symbols.name: t_\alpha
symbols.def: The value of \(\theta_n\) for sign schedule \(\alpha\).

symbols.name: s_{\alpha z}
symbols.def: The sign-valued outcome vector generated by schedule \(\alpha\) at assignment \(z\in\Omega_n\).

symbols.name: \pi
symbols.def: The vector \(\pi=(\pi_z)_{z\in\Omega_n}\) of assignment probabilities.

symbols.name: \pi_z
symbols.def: The probability assigned to \(z\in\Omega_n\) by a candidate finite program solution.

symbols.name: C_n(\pi)
symbols.def: The maximum target separation of two sign schedules multiplied by the square root of their \(\pi\)-probability of producing the same observation.

symbols.name: d_n(z,s)
symbols.def: The range of sign-schedule targets among schedules producing sign observation \(s\) at assignment \(z\), with value zero on singleton fibers.

symbols.name: U_n(\pi)
symbols.def: The largest, over sign schedules, root mean squared target-fiber diameter under \(\pi\).

symbols.name: w_{zs}
symbols.def: The product of \(\pi_z\) and the finite estimator value associated with observation cell \((z,s)\).

symbols.name: q_{\alpha z}
symbols.def: An epigraph variable for schedule \(\alpha\)'s squared loss at assignment \(z\).

symbols.name: r
symbols.def: The primal epigraph objective.

symbols.name: \mathsf P_n
symbols.def: The primal program in \(\mathrm{def{:}finite\text{-}primal}\).

symbols.name: \mu_\alpha
symbols.def: The dual probability mass placed on sign schedule \(\alpha\).

symbols.name: a_{zs}
symbols.def: The prior mass of sign schedules producing observation \(s\) at assignment \(z\).

symbols.name: b_{zs}
symbols.def: The unnormalized first target moment in observation cell \((z,s)\).

symbols.name: c_{zs}
symbols.def: The unnormalized second target moment in observation cell \((z,s)\).

symbols.name: u_{zs}
symbols.def: An epigraph coordinate satisfying \(a_{zs}u_{zs}\ge b_{zs}^2\).

symbols.name: v
symbols.def: The lower Bayes-risk objective common to every feasible assignment.

symbols.name: \mathsf Q_n
symbols.def: The least-favourable-prior dual in \(\mathrm{def{:}finite\text{-}dual}\).

symbols.name: \delta^{\mathrm{bin}}
symbols.def: The finite estimator recovered from a primal solution.

symbols.name: \delta^{\mathrm{ml}}
symbols.def: The Bernoulli multilinear extension of \(\delta^{\mathrm{bin}}\) to real bounded outcomes.

symbols.name: \Theta_n^\star
symbols.def: The design with masses given by an optimal primal solution.

symbols.name: \widehat\theta_n^\star
symbols.def: The multilinear estimator recovered from an optimal primal solution.

symbols.name: H_n(e)
symbols.def: Vertices \((i,k)\) and \((j,\ell)\) are adjacent when no \(z\in\Omega_n\) simultaneously realizes unit \(i\)'s exposure at \(\mathbf 0_n\) or \(\mathbf 1_n\), as selected by \(k\), and unit \(j\)'s corresponding endpoint exposure selected by \(\ell\).

symbols.name: e^{(0)}
symbols.def: The first mapping in the minimal witness table.

symbols.name: e^{(-)}
symbols.def: The second mapping in the lower-risk menu.

symbols.name: e^{(+)}
symbols.def: The second mapping in the higher-risk menu.

symbols.name: B
symbols.def: The integer with \(n=2B\) in the persistent witness sequence; for fixed \(\bar p\), the construction uses those \(B\) for which \(2B\in\mathcal N_{\bar p}\).

symbols.name: \rho_B
symbols.def: The common selector that preserves the two endpoints and otherwise reports whether unit \((1,1)\) is treated.

symbols.name: \widetilde e^{\kappa}
symbols.def: The mapping that applies the base coordinate \(e^{(\kappa)}_{a,2}\) to \(\rho_B(z)\) for every replicated unit \((j,a)\).

symbols.name: \widetilde{\mathcal E}_{B,-}
symbols.def: The menu \(\{\widetilde e^0,\widetilde e^-\}\).

symbols.name: \widetilde{\mathcal E}_{B,+}
symbols.def: The menu \(\{\widetilde e^0,\widetilde e^+\}\).

symbols.name: \delta_-
symbols.def: The explicit estimator for menu \(\mathcal E_-\).

symbols.name: \delta_+
symbols.def: The explicit estimator for menu \(\mathcal E_+\).

symbols.name: e^{\mathrm{loc}}
symbols.def: Unit \(1\) has exposure \(z_1\), while every other unit has constant exposure zero.

symbols.name: e^{\mathrm c}
symbols.def: Every unit has exposure zero at every assignment.

symbols.name: \mathcal E^{\mathrm{loc}}
symbols.def: The menu \(\{e^{\mathrm{loc}},e^{\mathrm c}\}\).

symbols.name: \widehat\theta^{\mathrm{loc}}
symbols.def: The explicit estimator for \(\mathcal E^{\mathrm{loc}}\).

symbols.name: e^{\mathrm{all}}
symbols.def: Every unit has exposure \(e^{\mathrm{all}}_{i,n}(z)=\mathbf 1\{z=\mathbf 1_n\}\).

symbols.name: \mathcal E^{\mathrm{nl}}
symbols.def: The menu \(\{e^{\mathrm{all}},e^{\mathrm c}\}\).

symbols.name: \widehat\theta^{\mathrm{nl}}
symbols.def: The explicit estimator for \(\mathcal E^{\mathrm{nl}}\).

symbols.name: e^{\mathrm{NI}}
symbols.def: The coordinate mapping \(e^{\mathrm{NI}}_{i,n}(z)=z_i\).

symbols.name: \mathcal E^{\mathrm{NI}}
symbols.def: The singleton menu \(\{e^{\mathrm{NI}}\}\).

symbols.name: \Theta_n^{\mathrm{CR}}
symbols.def: The uniform distribution on \(\Omega_n\).

symbols.name: \widehat\theta_n^{\mathrm{DM}}
symbols.def: The treated observed mean minus the control observed mean.

symbols.name: V_n^\star(\mathcal E,\bar p)
symbols.def: For \(n\in\mathcal N_{\bar p}\), the infimum over \(\Theta\in\mathcal D_n(\bar p)\) and arbitrary \(\widehat\theta\) of the worst-case root mean squared error over \(\mathcal Y_n(\mathcal E)\); its complete primitive index is \((n,\mathcal E,\bar p)\).

symbols.name: L_n(\mathcal E,\bar p)
symbols.def: The square root of the optimal objective of \(\mathsf P_n\), equivalently of \(\mathsf Q_n\), whose complete primitive index is \((n,\mathcal E,\bar p)\).

assumptions.condition: The table \(y\) is fixed before \(Z\sim\Theta\) is drawn.
There exist \(e\in\mathcal E\) and functions \(h_{i,e,n}:\mathcal X_{i,e,n}\to\mathbb R\) such that \(y_i(z)=h_{i,e,n}(e_{i,n}(z))\) for every \(i\in V_n\) and \(z\in\mathcal A_n\).

novel.justification: A short menu of scientifically interpretable neighborhood, threshold, and weighted-exposure summaries is realistic when domain knowledge narrows spillover propagation without selecting one summary as correct.

definitions.name: finite exposure-menu outcome class
definitions.construction: For fixed \(\bar p\in(0,1)\) and \(n\in\mathcal N_{\bar p}\), \(\mathcal Y_n(\mathcal E)=\{y=(y_i)_{i\in V_n}:y_i:\mathcal A_n\to[-1,1],\ y\text{ satisfies }\mathrm{ass{:}fixed\text{-}schedule},\mathrm{ass{:}bounded\text{-}table},\mathrm{ass{:}menu\text{-}measurability}\}\).

definitions.name: exact-budget design set
definitions.construction: For fixed \(\bar p\in(0,1)\) and \(n\in\mathcal N_{\bar p}\), \(\mathcal D_n(\bar p)=\{\Theta:\Theta(\Omega_n)=1\}\).

definitions.name: one-shot observed experiment
definitions.construction: For fixed \(\bar p\in(0,1)\) and \(n\in\mathcal N_{\bar p}\), draw \(Z\sim\Theta\), then reveal \(\mathsf O_n=(Z,(y_i(Z))_{i\in V_n})\) once.

definitions.name: design-inclusive ambiguity risk
finite sign-schedule experiment
definitions.construction: For fixed \(\bar p\in(0,1)\) and \(n\in\mathcal N_{\bar p}\), \(\mathcal B_n(\mathcal E)=\{\alpha=(e,b):e\in\mathcal E,\ b=(b_{i,x})_{i\in V_n,x\in\mathcal X_{i,e,n}}\in\{-1,1\}^{d_{e,n}}\}\); for \(\alpha=(e,b)\), set \(t_\alpha=n^{-1}\sum_{i\in V_n}[b_{i,e_{i,n}(\mathbf 1_n)}-b_{i,e_{i,n}(\mathbf 0_n)}]\) and \(s_{\alpha z}=(b_{i,e_{i,n}(z)})_{i\in V_n}\in\mathcal S_n\).

definitions.name: design-weighted collision geometry
definitions.construction: For fixed \(\bar p\in(0,1)\) and \(n\in\mathcal N_{\bar p}\), and for every design vector \(\pi\) on \(\Omega_n\), define \(C_n(\pi)=\max_{\alpha,\beta\in\mathcal B_n(\mathcal E)}|t_\alpha-t_\beta|\{\sum_{z\in\Omega_n:s_{\alpha z}=s_{\beta z}}\pi_z\}^{1/2}\). For every observation cell set \(d_n(z,s)=\max_{\alpha:s_{\alpha z}=s}t_\alpha-\min_{\alpha:s_{\alpha z}=s}t_\alpha\), with diameter zero for a singleton fiber, and define \(U_n(\pi)=\{\max_{\alpha\in\mathcal B_n(\mathcal E)}\sum_{z\in\Omega_n}\pi_z d_n(z,s_{\alpha z})^2\}^{1/2}\).

definitions.name: finite primal risk program
definitions.construction: For fixed \(\bar p\in(0,1)\) and \(n\in\mathcal N_{\bar p}\), \(\mathsf P_n\) has complete primitive data \((n,\mathcal E,\bar p)\) through \(\Omega_n\), \(\mathcal B_n(\mathcal E)\), \(s_{\alpha z}\), and \(t_\alpha\). It minimizes \(r\) over \(\pi_z\ge0\), \(w_{zs}\in\mathbb R\), and \(q_{\alpha z}\ge0\), subject to \(\sum_{z\in\Omega_n}\pi_z=1\), \(-2\pi_z\le w_{zs}\le2\pi_z\), \(\sum_{z\in\Omega_n}q_{\alpha z}\le r\) for every \(\alpha\in\mathcal B_n(\mathcal E)\), and the rotated-cone inequalities \(\pi_zq_{\alpha z}\ge(w_{z,s_{\alpha z}}-\pi_zt_\alpha)^2\) for every \((\alpha,z)\). The closed perspective convention forces \(w_{zs}=0\) when \(\pi_z=0\).

definitions.name: least-favourable-prior dual program
definitions.construction: For fixed \(\bar p\in(0,1)\) and \(n\in\mathcal N_{\bar p}\), \(\mathsf Q_n\) has complete primitive data \((n,\mathcal E,\bar p)\) through \(\Omega_n\), \(\mathcal B_n(\mathcal E)\), \(\mathcal S_n\), \(s_{\alpha z}\), and \(t_\alpha\). It maximizes \(v\) over \(\mu_\alpha\ge0\), \(a_{zs}\ge0\), \(b_{zs}\in\mathbb R\), \(c_{zs}\ge0\), and \(u_{zs}\ge0\), subject to \(\sum_\alpha\mu_\alpha=1\), \(a_{zs}=\sum_{\alpha:s_{\alpha z}=s}\mu_\alpha\), \(b_{zs}=\sum_{\alpha:s_{\alpha z}=s}\mu_\alpha t_\alpha\), \(c_{zs}=\sum_{\alpha:s_{\alpha z}=s}\mu_\alpha t_\alpha^2\), \(a_{zs}u_{zs}\ge b_{zs}^2\), and \(v\le\sum_{s\in\mathcal S_n}(c_{zs}-u_{zs})\) for every \(z\in\Omega_n\).

definitions.name: lossless estimator extension
definitions.construction: For fixed \(\bar p\in(0,1)\) and \(n\in\mathcal N_{\bar p}\), for \(z\in\Omega_n\) and \(x\in[-1,1]^n\), define \(\delta^{\mathrm{ml}}(z,x)=\sum_{s\in\mathcal S_n}\delta^{\mathrm{bin}}(z,s)\prod_{i\in V_n}(1+s_ix_i)/2\).

definitions.name: design and estimator recovery
definitions.construction: For fixed \(\bar p\in(0,1)\) and \(n\in\mathcal N_{\bar p}\), from an optimal primal solution set \(\Theta_n^\star(z)=\pi_z\), set \(\delta^{\mathrm{bin}}(z,s)=w_{zs}/\pi_z\) when \(\pi_z>0\) and zero when \(\pi_z=0\), and set \(\widehat\theta_n^\star=\delta^{\mathrm{ml}}\) using \(\mathrm{def{:}multilinear\text{-}extension}\).

definitions.name: minimal exact-budget mapping tables
definitions.construction:
On the unconditional two-unit assignment cube \(\{00,10,01,11\}\), define three binary exposure mappings independently of the treatment-budget fraction.  Every exposure range below is exactly \(\{0,1\}\), and every unit's endpoint exposures are distinct.  In row order \(00,10,01,11\), set
\[
 (e^{(0)}_{1,2},e^{(0)}_{2,2})=((0,0),(0,0),(0,1),(1,1)),
\]
\[
 (e^{(-)}_{1,2},e^{(-)}_{2,2})=((0,0),(0,0),(1,0),(1,1)),
\]
and
\[
 (e^{(+)}_{1,2},e^{(+)}_{2,2})=((0,0),(1,0),(0,0),(1,1)).
\]
Set \(\mathcal E_-=\{e^{(0)},e^{(-)}\}\) and \(\mathcal E_+=\{e^{(0)},e^{(+)}\}\).  Separately, for the minimal admissible exact-budget experiment, fix \(\bar p\in[1/2,1)\) and take \(n=2\).  Then \(m_2=\lfloor2\bar p\rfloor=1\), \(2\in\mathcal N_{\bar p}\), the graph \(G_2\) is empty, \(\mathcal A_2=\{00,10,01,11\}\), and \(\Omega_2=\{10,01\}\).

definitions.name: minimal witness conflict graphs
definitions.construction: Write \(a=(1,0)\), \(b=(1,1)\), \(c=(2,0)\), and \(d=(2,1)\). Then \(H_2(e^{(0)})\) has vertex set \(\{a,b,c,d\}\) and edge set \(\{ab,bc,bd,cd\}\), while both \(H_2(e^{(-)})\) and \(H_2(e^{(+)})\) have edge set \(\{ab,ad,bd,cd\}\). The menu isomorphisms are the identity on \(a,b,c,d\) from the shared \(H_2(e^{(0)})\) to itself and the identity from \(H_2(e^{(-)})\) to \(H_2(e^{(+)})\).

definitions.name: full bounded witness response arrays
definitions.construction: For \(\mathcal E_-\), schedule \(A\) under \(e^{(0)}\) has response coordinates \((h_{1}(0),h_{1}(1),h_{2}(0),h_{2}(1))=(-1,1,1,1)\), induced outcomes \((-1,1),(-1,1),(-1,1),(1,1)\) at \(00,10,01,11\), and target \(1\). Schedule \(B\) under \(e^{(-)}\) has coordinates \((-1,-1,1,-1)\), induced outcomes \((-1,1),(-1,1),(-1,1),(-1,-1)\), and target \(-1\). Thus the two schedules agree on every feasible assignment. For \(\mathcal E_+\), an explicit least-favourable sign prior places mass \(15/112\) on each \(e^{(0)}\) coordinate vector \((-1,-1,1,-1)\) and \((1,1,-1,1)\), mass \(5/32\) on each \(e^{(0)}\) vector \((-1,1,1,1)\) and \((1,-1,-1,-1)\), mass \(5/224\) on each \(e^{(+)}\) vector \((-1,-1,1,-1)\) and \((1,1,-1,1)\), and mass \(3/16\) on each \(e^{(+)}\) vector \((-1,1,-1,1)\) and \((1,-1,1,-1)\). The eight masses sum to one; their targets are respectively \((-1,1,1,-1,-1,1,2,-2)\). Conditional target means equal \(-3s_2/4\) at \(z=10\) and \(-3s_1/4\) at \(z=01\), and the conditional target variance averaged over either assignment is \(25/16\).

definitions.name: matching witness upper certificates
definitions.construction: For \(\mathcal E_-\), put all design mass on \(z=10\) and set \(\delta_-(10,x)=-(x_1+x_2)/2\). For \(\mathcal E_+\), use the uniform design on \(\{10,01\}\) and set \(\delta_+(10,x)=-3x_2/4\) and \(\delta_+(01,x)=-3x_1/4\). The latter rule has worst-case mean squared error \(25/16\) on each mapping, as certified by checking the sixteen sign vertices for each candidate and then applying \(\mathrm{lem{:}sign\text{-}reduction}\).

definitions.name: persistent even-population common-selector blow-up
definitions.construction:
Fix \(\bar p\in(0,1)\).  For \(B\ge1\) such that \(n=2B\in\mathcal N_{\bar p}\), label the units \((j,a)\) with \(j\in\{1,\ldots,B\}\) and \(a\in\{1,2\}\), take the empty graph, and set \(m_{2B}=\lfloor2B\bar p\rfloor\).  Define \(\rho_B:\mathcal A_{2B}\to\{00,10,01,11\}\) by
\[
 \rho_B(z)=
 \begin{cases}
 00,&z=\mathbf 0_{2B},\\
 11,&z=\mathbf 1_{2B},\\
 10,&z\notin\{\mathbf 0_{2B},\mathbf 1_{2B}\}\text{ and }z_{(1,1)}=1,\\
 01,&z\notin\{\mathbf 0_{2B},\mathbf 1_{2B}\}\text{ and }z_{(1,1)}=0.
 \end{cases}
\]
For \(\kappa\in\{0,-,+\}\), set
\[
 \widetilde e^{\kappa}_{(j,a),2B}(z)
 =e^{(\kappa)}_{a,2}(\rho_B(z)),
\]
and define \(\widetilde{\mathcal E}_{B,-}=\{\widetilde e^0,\widetilde e^-\}\) and \(\widetilde{\mathcal E}_{B,+}=\{\widetilde e^0,\widetilde e^+\}\).

definitions.name: graph-local vanishing-risk menu
definitions.construction: For fixed \(\bar p\in(0,1)\) and \(n\in\mathcal N_{\bar p}\), on the empty graph define \(e^{\mathrm{loc}}_{1,n}(z)=z_1\), \(e^{\mathrm{loc}}_{i,n}(z)=0\) for \(i\ge2\), and \(e^{\mathrm c}_{i,n}(z)=0\) for every \(i\). Set \(\mathcal E^{\mathrm{loc}}=\{e^{\mathrm{loc}},e^{\mathrm c}\}\), use any design in \(\mathcal D_n(\bar p)\), and define \(\widehat\theta^{\mathrm{loc}}(Z,Y^{\mathrm{obs}})=(2Z_1-1)Y_1^{\mathrm{obs}}/n\).

definitions.name: nonlocal positive-risk menu
definitions.construction: For fixed \(\bar p\in(0,1)\) and \(n\in\mathcal N_{\bar p}\), define \(e^{\mathrm{all}}_{i,n}(z)=\mathbf 1\{z=\mathbf 1_n\}\) and \(\mathcal E^{\mathrm{nl}}=\{e^{\mathrm{all}},e^{\mathrm c}\}\). Use any design in \(\mathcal D_n(\bar p)\) and define \(\widehat\theta^{\mathrm{nl}}(Z,Y^{\mathrm{obs}})=-n^{-1}\sum_{i\in V_n}Y_i^{\mathrm{obs}}\).

definitions.name: no-interference calibration design
definitions.construction: For fixed \(\bar p\in(0,1)\) and \(n\in\mathcal N_{\bar p}\), \(\Theta_n^{\mathrm{CR}}(z)=|\Omega_n|^{-1}\) for every \(z\in\Omega_n\).

definitions.name: no-interference calibration estimator
definitions.construction: For fixed \(\bar p\in(0,1)\) and \(n\in\mathcal N_{\bar p}\), \(\widehat\theta_n^{\mathrm{DM}}=m_n^{-1}\sum_{i\in V_n}Z_iY_i^{\mathrm{obs}}-(n-m_n)^{-1}\sum_{i\in V_n}(1-Z_i)Y_i^{\mathrm{obs}}\).

definitions.name: structural frontier handle
definitions.construction: Start from the explicit pairwise collision modulus \(C_n(\pi)\) and fiber-diameter modulus \(U_n(\pi)\), quotient their sign schedules and observation cells by automorphisms of the menu-induced sign experiment, and compare the optimized moduli with posterior-variance certificates from \(\mathsf Q_n\) to seek exposure-incidence summaries controlling \(L_n(\mathcal E,\bar p)\) without enumerating all sign schedules. The ambient graph \(G_n\) is not an argument of the unrestricted frontier. In graph-local subclasses it may constrain or organize an analyst-specified menu \(\mathcal E(G_n)\), or certify actions, orbits, and incidence bounds; every resulting effect on the frontier is mediated through that menu-induced finite experiment.

definitions.name: mapping-known oracle benchmark
definitions.construction:
For fixed \(\bar p\in(0,1)\), \(n\in\mathcal N_{\bar p}\), and a finite nonempty menu \(\mathcal E\), the mapping-known oracle benchmark is
\[
 \max_{e\in\mathcal E}V_n^\star(\{e\},\bar p),
\]
where \(V_n^\star(\{e\},\bar p)\) is the design-inclusive minimax root mean squared error in \(\mathrm{def{:}minimax\text{-}risk}\) with the adversarial menu restricted to the singleton \(\{e\}\). The design still ranges over all of \(\mathcal D_n(\bar p)\), and the estimator may depend on the known singleton mapping. Finiteness and nonemptiness of \(\mathcal E\) make the displayed maximum well defined.

statements.statement: Fix \(\bar p\in(0,1)\) and \(n\in\mathcal N_{\bar p}\). The minimax mean squared error over \(\mathcal Y_n(\mathcal E)\) equals the minimax mean squared error over the finite sign schedules \(\mathcal B_n(\mathcal E)\). More precisely, every rule \(\delta^{\mathrm{bin}}\) on \(\Omega_n\times\mathcal S_n\) has the multilinear extension in \(\mathrm{def{:}multilinear\text{-}extension}\), and for every \(e\in\mathcal E\) and every bounded response array \(h\), its risk is at most the largest risk of \(\delta^{\mathrm{bin}}\) over sign arrays for that same \(e\). Conversely, sign schedules form a subclass of \(\mathcal Y_n(\mathcal E)\).
statements.justification: This is the value-preserving elimination theorem that converts arbitrary real response arrays and arbitrary measurable estimators into a certified finite decision problem.
statements.gap: Kandiros, Harshaw, and Sävje (2026), Section 2.3, Proposition 2.2; restated and proved in Appendix A.5, show that for an interference network \(G\), a fixed contrastive effect \(\tau\), and \(q\ge2\), there exists a function \(f_q\) on labeled graphs such that \(R(G,\tau,q)=f_q(H)\) for the single known model's conflict graph \(H\); they do not reduce a latent finite union, cross-model collisions, or the present exact-treated-count slice.
statements.consumer: The finite reduction permits exact numerical certification without imposing linearity, unbiasedness, graph locality, or finitely valued observed outcomes.
statements.proof_tex:
Fix a design \(\Theta\), and write \(\pi_z=\Theta(Z=z)\).  Projection of any estimate onto \([-2,2]\) cannot increase squared error because every target \(\theta_n(y)\) lies in \([-2,2]\).  It is therefore enough to consider rules with values in \([-2,2]\).

Fix \(e\in\mathcal E\) and a bounded response array \(h=(h_{i,e,n}(x))\).  For every response coordinate \((i,x)\), independently draw a sign \(B_{i,x}\in\{-1,1\}\) with
\[
 \mathbb P(B_{i,x}=1)=\frac{1+h_{i,e,n}(x)}2,
 \qquad
 \mathbb E B_{i,x}=h_{i,e,n}(x).
\]
This is well-defined by \(\mathrm{ass{:}bounded\text{-}table}\).  The random pair \((e,B)\) is a sign schedule in \(\mathcal B_n(\mathcal E)\).  For fixed \(z\in\Omega_n\), independence across the unit-indexed response coordinates gives
\[
 \mathbb E_B\!\left[\delta^{\mathrm{bin}}(z,s_{(e,B)z})\right]
 =\sum_{s\in\mathcal S_n}\delta^{\mathrm{bin}}(z,s)
   \prod_{i\in V_n}\frac{1+s_i h_{i,e,n}(e_{i,n}(z))}{2}
 =\delta^{\mathrm{ml}}\bigl(z,(h_{i,e,n}(e_{i,n}(z)))_{i\in V_n}\bigr),
\]
where the last equality is \(\mathrm{def{:}multilinear\text{-}extension}\).  Linearity of the endpoint contrast similarly gives
\[
 \mathbb E_B t_{(e,B)}
 =\frac1n\sum_{i\in V_n}
   \left[h_{i,e,n}(e_{i,n}(\mathbf 1_n))-h_{i,e,n}(e_{i,n}(\mathbf 0_n))\right]
 =\theta_n(y).
\]
The last equality uses \(\mathrm{ass{:}menu\text{-}measurability}\) and \(\mathrm{def{:}ambiguity\text{-}class}\).  Jensen's inequality for the square, applied separately at every \(z\), now yields
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 &\left\{\delta^{\mathrm{ml}}(z,Y^{\mathrm{obs}}(z))-\theta_n(y)\right\}^2\\
 &\quad=\left\{\mathbb E_B[\delta^{\mathrm{bin}}(z,s_{(e,B)z})-t_{(e,B)}]\right\}^2\\
 &\quad\le \mathbb E_B\left[\{\delta^{\mathrm{bin}}(z,s_{(e,B)z})-t_{(e,B)}\}^2\right].
 \end{aligned}
\]
Multiplying by \(\pi_z\), summing over \(z\), and interchanging two finite sums proves
\[
 \mathbb E_{Z\sim\Theta}\!\left[
   \{\delta^{\mathrm{ml}}(\mathsf O_n)-\theta_n(y)\}^2\right]
 \le
 \max_{b\in\{-1,1\}^{d_{e,n}}}
 \sum_{z\in\Omega_n}\pi_z
   \{\delta^{\mathrm{bin}}(z,s_{(e,b)z})-t_{(e,b)}\}^2.
\]
This proves the asserted upper reduction for each candidate \(e\), hence for their finite union.  Conversely, every sign array is a bounded fixed response array measurable with respect to its displayed candidate mapping, so it belongs to \(\mathcal Y_n(\mathcal E)\) by the three assumptions defining that class.  Restricting an arbitrary real-outcome rule to sign observations therefore gives the reverse minimax inequality.  Taking the infimum over rules, and also over designs when desired, proves equality of the two minimax mean squared errors.

statements.statement:
Fix \(\bar p\in(0,1)\) and \(n\in\mathcal N_{\bar p}\). The complete primitive data of \(\mathsf P_n\) and \(\mathsf Q_n\) are \((n,\mathcal E,\bar p)\), and the two programs attain equal optimal objectives. With \(L_n(\mathcal E,\bar p)\) equal to the square root of this common objective, one has
\[
 V_n^\star(\mathcal E,\bar p)=L_n(\mathcal E,\bar p)
 =\sqrt{\operatorname{val}(\mathsf P_n)}
 =\sqrt{\operatorname{val}(\mathsf Q_n)}.
\]
The recovery in \(\mathrm{def{:}primal\text{-}recovery}\) yields \(\Theta_n^\star\in\mathcal D_n(\bar p)\) and an arbitrary-outcome estimator \(\widehat\theta_n^\star\) satisfying
\[
 \sup_{y\in\mathcal Y_n(\mathcal E)}
 \operatorname{RMSE}_n(\Theta_n^\star,\widehat\theta_n^\star;y)
 =L_n(\mathcal E,\bar p).
\]
Every \(\Theta\in\mathcal D_n(\bar p)\) and every measurable \(\widehat\theta\) have worst-case root mean squared error at least \(L_n(\mathcal E,\bar p)\). Holding \((n,\mathcal E,\bar p)\) fixed, the outcome model, exact-budget design class, finite decision experiment, programs, set of recovered optimal design--rule pairs, and exact minimax value are unchanged when the ambient known graph \(G_n\) changes. In particular, the same optimal primal solution recovers the same pair. Allowing a rule to read a fixed known \(G_n\) does not change the unrestricted decision-rule class, because that fixed constant can be compiled into the rule.
statements.proof_tex:
\textbf{Proof.}
Let \(A=\mathcal B_n(\mathcal E)\). It is finite. Since \(t_\alpha\in[-2,2]\), projection of an estimate onto \([-2,2]\) cannot increase square loss. For \(z\in\Omega_n\) and \(d=(d_s)_{s\in\mathcal S_n}\in[-2,2]^{\mathcal S_n}\), define
\[
 \ell(z,d)_\alpha=(d_{s_{\alpha z}}-t_\alpha)^2,
 \qquad \alpha\in A,
\]
and let \(K\subset\mathbb R^A\) be the convex hull of these loss vectors. Finiteness of \(A,\Omega_n,\mathcal S_n\) and compactness of the rule cube make \(K\) compact and convex. Randomization over rules conditional on \(z\) can be replaced by the conditional mean rule, because the square is convex coordinatewise. Conversely, a design \(\pi\) and assignment-specific rules give a distribution over \((z,d)\). Thus the sign-experiment minimax mean squared error is
\[
 R_n=\min_{x\in K}\max_{\alpha\in A}x_\alpha. \tag{1}
\]

We prove the required finite minimax equality rather than assume it. Put \(\rho=R_n\). For \(\varepsilon>0\), the compact convex set \(K\) and the closed convex lower orthant
\[
 D_\varepsilon=\{q:q_\alpha\le\rho-\varepsilon\text{ for every }\alpha\}
\]
are disjoint. Let \((x_\varepsilon,q_\varepsilon)\) be a closest pair and put \(h_\varepsilon=x_\varepsilon-q_\varepsilon\). The first-order inequalities for squared distance along line segments are
\[
 h_\varepsilon^{\mathsf T}(x-x_\varepsilon)\ge0\quad(x\in K),
 \qquad
 h_\varepsilon^{\mathsf T}(q-q_\varepsilon)\le0\quad(q\in D_\varepsilon). \tag{2}
\]
The negative coordinate rays of \(D_\varepsilon\) imply \(h_{\varepsilon,\alpha}\ge0\); whenever this coordinate is positive, the upper face constraint is active, so \(q_{\varepsilon,\alpha}=\rho-\varepsilon\). Normalizing \(h_\varepsilon\) gives a prior \(\mu^\varepsilon\) with
\[
 \min_{x\in K}\sum_\alpha\mu^\varepsilon_\alpha x_\alpha
 \ge \rho-\varepsilon. \tag{3}
\]
A convergent subsequence as \(\varepsilon\downarrow0\), compactness of the prior simplex, and continuity yield a prior attaining at least \(\rho\). The reverse inequality follows from \(\sum_\alpha\mu_\alpha x_\alpha\le\max_\alpha x_\alpha\). Hence
\[
 R_n=\max_{\mu\in\Delta(A)}
 \min_{z\in\Omega_n,\ d\in[-2,2]^{\mathcal S_n}}
 \sum_{\alpha\in A}\mu_\alpha(d_{s_{\alpha z}}-t_\alpha)^2. \tag{4}
\]

Fix \((\mu,z)\). In cell \((z,s)\), the objective is
\[
 a_{zs}d_s^2-2b_{zs}d_s+c_{zs}. \tag{5}
\]
If \(a_{zs}>0\), its minimizer is \(b_{zs}/a_{zs}\in[-2,2]\), with minimum \(c_{zs}-b_{zs}^2/a_{zs}\). If \(a_{zs}=0\), the defining nonnegative sums give \(b_{zs}=c_{zs}=0\). Therefore, with \(0/0=0\),
\[
 R_n=\max_{\mu\in\Delta(A)}\min_{z\in\Omega_n}
 \sum_{s\in\mathcal S_n}
 \left(c_{zs}-\frac{b_{zs}^2}{a_{zs}}\right). \tag{6}
\]
The rotated-cone constraints in \(\mathsf Q_n\) encode (6) exactly: maximization chooses \(u_{zs}=b_{zs}^2/a_{zs}\) for positive \(a_{zs}\) and zero otherwise. Since \(|b_{zs}|\le2a_{zs}\), the convention is continuous at zero. Compactness of the prior simplex and finiteness of the cell sets prove dual attainment and \(\operatorname{val}(\mathsf Q_n)=R_n\).

For the primal, any feasible \((\pi,w,q,r)\) gives \(d_{zs}=w_{zs}/\pi_z\in[-2,2]\) when \(\pi_z>0\), and
\[
 q_{\alpha z}\ge\pi_z(d_{z,s_{\alpha z}}-t_\alpha)^2. \tag{7}
\]
When \(\pi_z=0\), the closed perspective forces \(w_{zs}=0\) and the cell contributes no design loss. Conversely, any \((\pi,d)\) yields a feasible point by
\[
 w_{zs}=\pi_zd_{zs},\qquad
 q_{\alpha z}=\pi_z(d_{z,s_{\alpha z}}-t_\alpha)^2,
 \qquad
 r=\max_\alpha\sum_zq_{\alpha z}. \tag{8}
\]
Equations (1), (7), and (8) give
\[
 \operatorname{val}(\mathsf P_n)=R_n=\operatorname{val}(\mathsf Q_n). \tag{9}
\]
The compact minimizer in (1), conditional-mean derandomization, and (8) prove primal attainment.

The recovered \(\pi\) is a probability vector on the nonempty \(\Omega_n\), hence defines \(\Theta_n^\star\in\mathcal D_n(\bar p)\). The recovered sign rule has worst-case mean squared error \(R_n\). By \(\mathrm{lem{:}sign\text{-}reduction}\), its multilinear extension has risk at most \(R_n\) on all bounded tables, and the sign schedules, being a subclass, give the reverse inequality. Thus
\[
 V_n^\star(\mathcal E,\bar p)=\sqrt{R_n}
 =L_n(\mathcal E,\bar p),
\]
the recovered pair attains the value, and the definition of the infimum gives the asserted converse for every individual design and rule.

Finally, inspect the primitive data. Once \((n,\mathcal E,\bar p)\) is fixed, \(\Omega_n\), \(\mathcal Y_n(\mathcal E)\), \(A\), \(t_\alpha\), \(s_{\alpha z}\), both programs, and the recovery formulas contain no \(G_n\). For a fixed graph \(g\), a rule allowed to read it has the form \((z,x)\mapsto f(z,x,g)\); defining \(f_g(z,x)=f(z,x,g)\) shows it is an ordinary measurable map on \(\Omega_n\times[-1,1]^n\). Conversely every ordinary rule is allowed. Hence the rule class is identical for every fixed ambient graph. The same optimal program solution may therefore be used after changing \(G_n\), proving all invariance claims. The only boundary condition used is \(n\in\mathcal N_{\bar p}\), which makes \(\Omega_n\) finite and nonempty; no assignment-level positivity, rank, locality, or further boundary condition is required. \(\square\)

statements.statement: Fix \(\bar p\in[1/2,1)\), so \(m_2=\lfloor2\bar p\rfloor=1\). The construction in \(\mathrm{def{:}minimal\text{-}witness\text{-}mappings}\) is minimal: \(n=2\) and \(m_2=1\) are the smallest admissible population and budget because no integer satisfies \(1\le m\le n-1\) when \(n=1\). Both menus have cardinality two, every unit has distinct endpoint exposures under every mapping, and \(\{H_2(e):e\in\mathcal E_-\}\) and \(\{H_2(e):e\in\mathcal E_+\}\) are identical as multisets of labeled graphs under the explicit identity isomorphisms in \(\mathrm{def{:}minimal\text{-}witness\text{-}graphs}\). Nevertheless, the exact ambiguity minimax risks are \(V_2^\star(\mathcal E_-,\bar p)=1\) and \(V_2^\star(\mathcal E_+,\bar p)=5/4\). The two fully tabulated colliding arrays give the first matching lower certificate, the eight-point least-favourable prior gives the second, and the explicit designs and estimators in \(\mathrm{def{:}minimal\text{-}witness\text{-}estimators}\) give the matching upper certificates. Hence derived mapping-wise conflict graphs alone do not represent latent-menu risk on the exact-budget slice; this is not a claim of primitive dependence on the ambient graph.
statements.proof_tex:
\textbf{Proof.}
For \(\bar p\in[1/2,1)\), \(m_2=1\) and \(\Omega_2=\{10,01\}\). No integer budget is nondegenerate at \(n=1\), proving minimality. The endpoint rows \(00\) and \(11\) in \(\mathrm{def{:}minimal\text{-}witness\text{-}mappings}\) give exposure zero and one for every unit. With \(a=(1,0),b=(1,1),c=(2,0),d=(2,1)\), the feasible endpoint-vertex sets are \(\{a,c\},\{a,d\}\) for \(e^{(0)}\), and \(\{a,c\},\{b,c\}\) in opposite orders for \(e^{(-)}\) and \(e^{(+)}\). Their complements give exactly the edge sets in \(\mathrm{def{:}minimal\text{-}witness\text{-}graphs}\), so the asserted labeled identity isomorphisms hold.

For \(\mathcal E_-\), schedules \(A\) and \(B\) from \(\mathrm{def{:}minimal\text{-}witness\text{-}arrays}\) produce the same outcome \((-1,1)\) at both feasible assignments and have targets \(1\) and \(-1\). For any rule values \(D_z\) and any design \(\pi\),
\[
 \sum_z\pi_z\{(D_z-1)^2+(D_z+1)^2\}
 =2\sum_z\pi_zD_z^2+2\ge2,
\]
so the worst mean squared error is at least one. Put all mass on \(10\). For either lower-menu mapping, write the bounded response coordinates as \((a,b,c,d)\). The target is \(t=(b-a+d-c)/2\), whereas \(\delta_-(10,(a,c))=-(a+c)/2\), and the error is \(-(b+d)/2\), of absolute value at most one. Hence
\[
 V_2^\star(\mathcal E_-,\bar p)=1. \tag{1}
\]

For \(\mathcal E_+\), substitute the eight atoms and masses from \(\mathrm{def{:}minimal\text{-}witness\text{-}arrays}\) into the two exposure tables. Multiplying cell mass, first moment, and second moment by \(224\) gives
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c}
z&s&(224a_{zs},224b_{zs},224c_{zs})\\ \hline
10&(-1,1)&(112,-84,238)\\
10&(1,-1)&(112,84,238)\\
01&(-1,-1)&(72,54,198)\\
01&(1,1)&(72,-54,198)\\
01&(-1,1)&(40,30,40)\\
01&(1,-1)&(40,-30,40).
\end{array} \tag{2}
\]
Thus the posterior means are \(-3s_2/4\) at \(10\) and \(-3s_1/4\) at \(01\). The posterior-variance contributions are \(25/32,25/32\) at \(10\) and \(45/64,45/64,5/64,5/64\) at \(01\); they sum to \(25/16\) at either assignment. The posterior square-loss identity therefore gives mean squared error at least \(25/16\) for every rule under every design.

Conversely, under the uniform design use \(\delta_+(10,x)=-3x_2/4\) and \(\delta_+(01,x)=-3x_1/4\). For either mapping its risk at a sign vector \((a,b,c,d)\) is
\[
 \frac12\left(-\frac34c-t\right)^2
 +\frac12\left(-\frac34a-t\right)^2,
 \qquad t=\frac{b-a+d-c}{2}. \tag{3}
\]
Direct substitution over the sixteen sign vectors gives only \(1/16,9/16,25/16\). Expression (3) is separately convex in each coordinate, so successive endpoint maximization extends the same bound to \([-1,1]^4\). Hence
\[
 V_2^\star(\mathcal E_+,\bar p)=\frac54. \tag{4}
\]
Equations (1)--(4), together with \(\mathrm{thm{:}finite\text{-}saddle}\), prove the exact risks and certificates. Since the derived mapping-wise graph multisets agree while the risks differ, those graphs do not represent the latent-menu frontier. No ambient graph enters either risk calculation. \(\square\)

statements.statement:
Fix \(\bar p\in(0,1)\). For every \(B\ge1\) such that \(n=2B\in\mathcal N_{\bar p}\), put \(m_{2B}=\lfloor2B\bar p\rfloor\), so \(1\le m_{2B}\le2B-1\). The two menus in \(\mathrm{def{:}persistent\text{-}witness}\) have cardinality two, every unit retains distinct endpoint exposures, and \(\rho_B(\Omega_{2B})=\{10,01\}\). For each \(\kappa\in\{0,-,+\}\), \(H_{2B}(\widetilde e^\kappa)\) is the labeled type blow-up of \(H_2(e^{(\kappa)})\): vertices are \(((j,a),k)\), and two such vertices are adjacent exactly when no \(q\in\{10,01\}\) simultaneously realizes their two base endpoint exposures under \(e^{(\kappa)}\). In particular, the feasible endpoint-exposure vector sets of \(\widetilde e^-\) and \(\widetilde e^+\) coincide, and the identity map \(((j,a),k)\mapsto((j,a),k)\) is an explicit labeled graph isomorphism; the same identity matches the shared \(\widetilde e^0\) graphs. Thus the two mapping-wise labeled graph multisets agree. Their mapping-known oracle benchmarks coincide:
\[
 \max_{\kappa\in\{0,-\}}V_{2B}^\star(\{\widetilde e^\kappa\},\bar p)
 =\max_{\kappa\in\{0,+\}}V_{2B}^\star(\{\widetilde e^\kappa\},\bar p)
 =\frac56.
\]
Nevertheless,
\[
 V_{2B}^\star(\widetilde{\mathcal E}_{B,-},\bar p)=1,
 \qquad
 V_{2B}^\star(\widetilde{\mathcal E}_{B,+},\bar p)=\frac54.
\]
The corresponding additive adaptation prices are \(1/6\) and \(5/12\), and the robust-to-oracle risk ratios are \(6/5\) and \(3/2\). The lower certificates are uniform over every design in \(\mathcal D_{2B}(\bar p)\) and every measurable estimator, while explicit budget-feasible designs and block-averaged estimators attain all singleton and robust values for arbitrary block-specific bounded response coordinates. Consequently, for every fixed \(\bar p\in(0,1)\), every sufficiently large even population size belongs to \(\mathcal N_{\bar p}\); identical derived mapping-wise labeled conflict-graph multisets then conceal both a persistent robust-risk gap \(1/4\) and a persistent additive-adaptation-price gap \(1/4\). The separation concerns those menu-derived graphs, not primitive ambient-graph dependence.
statements.proof_tex:
\textbf{Proof.}
Put \(m=\lfloor2B\bar p\rfloor\). Admissibility gives \(1\le m\le2B-1\). Treating the distinguished unit and any \(m-1\) others realizes selector cell \(10\); leaving it untreated and treating any \(m\) remaining units realizes \(01\). Every feasible assignment is a nonendpoint, so
\[
 \rho_B(\Omega_{2B})=\{10,01\}. \tag{1}
\]
The selector maps the two endpoints to \(00\) and \(11\), and the base endpoint exposures are distinct, so every replica retains this property.

A replicated endpoint vertex \(((j,a),k)\) is realized by \(z\) precisely when \(e^{(\kappa)}_{a,2}(\rho_B(z))\) equals its base endpoint exposure. By (1), two replicated vertices are jointly realizable exactly when some \(q\in\{10,01\}\) realizes both base exposures. Negation gives the asserted blow-up adjacency rule. The base cells for \(e^{(-)}\) and \(e^{(+)}\) realize the same two endpoint-vertex sets in opposite order, so the identity is a labeled isomorphism; the \(\widetilde e^0\) graphs are literally shared.

Replicate schedules \(A\) and \(B\) from the minimal witness in every block. They agree on every feasible assignment and have normalized targets \(1\) and \(-1\). Hence for every rule value \(D_Z\),
\[
 \mathbb E[(D_Z-1)^2+(D_Z+1)^2]=2\mathbb E[D_Z^2]+2\ge2,
\]
so \(V_{2B}^\star(\widetilde{\mathcal E}_{B,-},\bar p)\ge1\). Put all design mass on a selector-\(10\) assignment, apply \(\delta_-\) blockwise, and average. In block \(j\), the error is \(-(b_j+d_j)/2\), whose absolute value is at most one; the average error is therefore bounded by one. Thus
\[
 V_{2B}^\star(\widetilde{\mathcal E}_{B,-},\bar p)=1. \tag{2}
\]

For the higher menu, draw one atom from the eight-point least-favourable prior and replicate it in every block. Conditional on any physical assignment, the observed vector is \(B\) copies of the base observation at \(\rho_B(z)\), while the normalized target is the base target. The posterior calculation in \(\mathrm{thm{:}minimal\text{-}nonrepresentability}\) gives Bayes mean squared error \(25/16\) at either selector cell, hence under every physical design. Conversely, put mass one half on one assignment from each selector cell, apply \(\delta_+\) blockwise, and average. Pointwise,
\[
 \left\{B^{-1}\sum_j(\widehat t_j-t_j)\right\}^2
 \le B^{-1}\sum_j(\widehat t_j-t_j)^2.
\]
Each expected block square is at most \(25/16\), even for block-specific bounded coordinates. Therefore
\[
 V_{2B}^\star(\widetilde{\mathcal E}_{B,+},\bar p)=\frac54. \tag{3}
\]

By \(\mathrm{prop{:}singleton\text{-}witness\text{-}oracle\text{-}values}\), both mapping-known benchmarks equal \(5/6\). Subtracting and dividing, which is valid because \(5/6>0\), yields
\[
 1-\frac56=\frac16,
 \quad \frac54-\frac56=\frac5{12},
 \quad \frac1{5/6}=\frac65,
 \quad \frac{5/4}{5/6}=\frac32.
\]
Both displayed gaps equal \(1/4\). Finally, for all sufficiently large \(B\), \(1\le\lfloor2B\bar p\rfloor\le2B-1\), so the construction persists along every fixed \(\bar p\in(0,1)\). The risk calculations depend on the menus and budget slice, not on the empty ambient graph used to present the witness. \(\square\)

statements.statement: Fix \(\bar p\in(0,1)\) and \(n\in\mathcal N_{\bar p}\). For the graph-local two-mapping menu \(\mathcal E^{\mathrm{loc}}\), the finite primal and dual solve to \(L_n(\mathcal E^{\mathrm{loc}},\bar p)=1/n\). The estimator in \(\mathrm{def{:}local\text{-}solved\text{-}menu}\) is optimal under every exact-budget design. A dual certificate places independent symmetric sign mass on the two response coordinates of unit \(1\), so whichever value is observed, the other contributes posterior target variance \(1/n^2\). The adjective graph-local describes how this menu was selected; the exact value is a functional of the resulting menu and budget.
statements.proof_tex:
\textbf{Proof.}
Under \(e^{\mathrm{loc}}\), write \(a\) and \(b\) for unit \(1\)'s responses at exposures zero and one. Every other endpoint contrast vanishes, and the constant mapping is a subclass, so every table in the union has
\[
 \theta_n(y)=\frac{b-a}{n}. \tag{1}
\]
If \(Z_1=1\), the displayed estimator is \(b/n\) and its error is \(a/n\); if \(Z_1=0\), it is \(-a/n\) and its error is \(-b/n\). Thus its error is pointwise bounded by \(1/n\) under every exact-budget design.

For the lower bound, take \(a,b\) independent symmetric signs and fix all other coordinates. Given any assignment and full observation, exactly one of \(a,b\) remains an independent unseen sign. By (1),
\[
 \operatorname{Var}(\theta_n(y)\mid Z,Y^{\mathrm{obs}})=n^{-2}.
\]
The posterior square-loss identity gives Bayes mean squared error at least \(n^{-2}\) for every design and rule; worst-case risk dominates this finite prior average. Therefore, by \(\mathrm{thm{:}finite\text{-}saddle}\),
\[
 L_n(\mathcal E^{\mathrm{loc}},\bar p)
 =V_n^\star(\mathcal E^{\mathrm{loc}},\bar p)=\frac1n.
\]
No assignment-level positivity is needed. \(\square\)

statements.statement: Fix \(\bar p\in(0,1)\) and \(n\in\mathcal N_{\bar p}\). For the genuinely nonlocal two-mapping menu \(\mathcal E^{\mathrm{nl}}\), the finite primal and dual solve to \(L_n(\mathcal E^{\mathrm{nl}},\bar p)=1\) for every \(n\in\mathcal N_{\bar p}\). The estimator in \(\mathrm{def{:}nonlocal\text{-}solved\text{-}menu}\) is optimal under every exact-budget design. Two schedules with identical zero outcomes on \(\Omega_n\) and all-treated response vectors \(\mathbf 1_n\) and \(-\mathbf 1_n\) give the dual lower certificate.
statements.proof_tex:
\textbf{Proof.}
Admissibility gives \(1\le m_n\le n-1\), so no feasible assignment is \(\mathbf 1_n\). Under \(e^{\mathrm{all}}\), write \(a_i=h_i(0)\) and \(b_i=h_i(1)\). Every feasible observation is \((a_i)_i\), while
\[
 \theta_n(y)=n^{-1}\sum_i(b_i-a_i). \tag{1}
\]
The constant model is contained in this model. The displayed estimator has error \(-n^{-1}\sum_i b_i\), of absolute value at most one, under every design.

For a lower certificate, place equal mass on two fixed schedules having \(a_i=0\) for all \(i\), and respectively \(b_i=1\) and \(b_i=-1\) for all \(i\). Their feasible observations agree and their targets are \(1\) and \(-1\). For any rule value \(D_z\),
\[
 \frac12(D_z-1)^2+\frac12(D_z+1)^2=D_z^2+1\ge1.
\]
Averaging under any design proves a Bayes and hence worst-case mean squared error lower bound of one. Thus
\[
 V_n^\star(\mathcal E^{\mathrm{nl}},\bar p)
 =L_n(\mathcal E^{\mathrm{nl}},\bar p)=1
\]
by \(\mathrm{thm{:}finite\text{-}saddle}\), and the displayed rule is optimal under every exact-budget design. \(\square\)

statements.statement:
Fix \(\bar p\in(0,1)\) and \(n\in\mathcal N_{\bar p}\). The primitive collision moduli satisfy
\[
 \frac12\inf_{\pi}C_n(\pi)
 \le V_n^\star(\mathcal E,\bar p)
 \le\frac12\inf_{\pi}U_n(\pi),
\]
where both infima range over the probability simplex on \(\Omega_n\). For the lower bound, on every assignment where schedules \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) collide, \((a-t_\alpha)^2+(a-t_\beta)^2\ge(t_\alpha-t_\beta)^2/2\), and the worse schedule has mean squared error at least one quarter of the squared collision modulus. For the upper bound, assign every sign observation cell the midpoint of its target interval, then apply the sign reduction and multilinear extension. Along \(n\in\mathcal N_{\bar p}\) with \(n\to\infty\), \(\inf_\pi U_n(\pi)\to0\) is sufficient for \(V_n^\star(\mathcal E,\bar p)\to0\), while \(V_n^\star(\mathcal E,\bar p)\to0\) implies \(\inf_\pi C_n(\pi)\to0\). A positive lower limit of \(\inf_\pi C_n(\pi)\) is sufficient for a positive lower limit of \(V_n^\star(\mathcal E,\bar p)\), while a positive lower limit of \(V_n^\star(\mathcal E,\bar p)\) implies a positive lower limit of \(\inf_\pi U_n(\pi)\).
statements.proof_tex:
\textbf{Proof.}
Fix a design vector \(\pi\) and an arbitrary rule. For schedules \(\alpha,\beta\), let \(E_{\alpha\beta}=\{z:s_{\alpha z}=s_{\beta z}\}\). On this event the two schedules produce the same observed experiment, so the rule takes a common value \(a_z\). The identity
\[
 (a_z-t_\alpha)^2+(a_z-t_\beta)^2
 =2\left(a_z-\frac{t_\alpha+t_\beta}{2}\right)^2
 +\frac{(t_\alpha-t_\beta)^2}{2}
 \ge\frac{(t_\alpha-t_\beta)^2}{2}
\]
shows, after weighting by \(\pi_z\) and summing, that the larger of the two full mean squared errors is at least
\[
 \frac{(t_\alpha-t_\beta)^2}{4}
 \sum_{z\in E_{\alpha\beta}}\pi_z.
\]
Sign schedules lie in \(\mathcal Y_n(\mathcal E)\), so maximizing over pairs and infimizing over rules and designs gives the lower bound.

For the upper bound, for each nonempty fiber \(F_{zs}=\{\alpha:s_{\alpha z}=s\}\), define
\[
 \delta^{\mathrm{bin}}(z,s)=\frac12
 \left(\max_{\alpha\in F_{zs}}t_\alpha+\min_{\alpha\in F_{zs}}t_\alpha\right).
\]
Finiteness makes the extrema well defined. For every schedule and assignment,
\[
 |\delta^{\mathrm{bin}}(z,s_{\alpha z})-t_\alpha|
 \le\frac12d_n(z,s_{\alpha z}),
\]
so its mean squared error is at most one quarter of the corresponding diameter sum. Maximizing over schedules gives root mean squared error at most \(U_n(\pi)/2\). The sign reduction and multilinear extension give an explicit arbitrary-outcome rule with no larger risk. Infimizing over \(\pi\) proves the upper bound.

Writing \(C_n^\circ=\inf_\pi C_n(\pi)\) and \(U_n^\circ=\inf_\pi U_n(\pi)\), the proved inequalities are exactly
\[
 C_n^\circ\le2V_n^\star(\mathcal E,\bar p)\le U_n^\circ.
\]
All four asymptotic implications follow immediately by taking limits or lower limits along the admissible sequence. These are one-sided certificates and do not assert a reverse comparison. Nonemptiness of \(\Omega_n\) is the only support condition; no assignment-level positivity, rank, locality, or additional boundary condition is used. \(\square\)

statements.statement: Fix \(\bar p\in(0,1)\) and \(n\in\mathcal N_{\bar p}\). For the singleton menu \(\mathcal E^{\mathrm{NI}}\), complete randomization and difference in means satisfy \(\sup_{y\in\mathcal Y_n(\mathcal E^{\mathrm{NI}})}\operatorname{RMSE}_n(\Theta_n^{\mathrm{CR}},\widehat\theta_n^{\mathrm{DM}};y)\le\{n(n-1)^{-1}[m_n^{-1}+(n-m_n)^{-1}]\}^{1/2}\). Along \(n\in\mathcal N_{\bar p}\) with \(n\to\infty\), the finite-program value obeys \(L_n(\mathcal E^{\mathrm{NI}},\bar p)\asymp n^{-1/2}\).
statements.proof_tex:
\textbf{Proof.}
For a no-interference table put \(a_i=y_i(\mathbf 0_n)\), \(b_i=y_i(\mathbf 1_n)\), and \(\tau_i=b_i-a_i\). The observed response is \(b_i\) when treated and \(a_i\) otherwise, and the target is \(\bar\tau=n^{-1}\sum_i\tau_i\). Under complete randomization, counting assignments containing one or two specified units gives
\[
 \mathbb EZ_i=\frac{m_n}{n},\quad
 \operatorname{Var}(Z_i)=\frac{m_n(n-m_n)}{n^2},\quad
 \operatorname{Cov}(Z_i,Z_j)=-\frac{m_n(n-m_n)}{n^2(n-1)}\quad(i\ne j). \tag{1}
\]
Consequently difference in means is unbiased and has Neyman variance
\[
 \operatorname{Var}(\widehat\theta_n^{\mathrm{DM}})
 =\frac{S_b^2}{m_n}+\frac{S_a^2}{n-m_n}-\frac{S_\tau^2}{n}, \tag{2}
\]
where each \(S^2\) uses denominator \(n-1\). Boundedness in an interval of length two gives \(S_a^2,S_b^2\le n/(n-1)\). Dropping the nonpositive final term in (2) proves
\[
 \sup_y\operatorname{RMSE}_n(\Theta_n^{\mathrm{CR}},\widehat\theta_n^{\mathrm{DM}};y)
 \le\left\{\frac{n}{n-1}
 \left(\frac1{m_n}+\frac1{n-m_n}\right)\right\}^{1/2}. \tag{3}
\]

For a design-uniform lower bound, place independent symmetric sign mass on the \(2n\) fixed endpoint responses. Conditional on any exact-budget assignment and all observed outcomes, one endpoint response per unit remains unobserved and independent. Therefore
\[
 \operatorname{Var}(\bar\tau\mid Z,Y^{\mathrm{obs}})=\frac1n. \tag{4}
\]
The posterior square-loss identity makes (4) a Bayes mean squared error lower bound for every design and rule. By \(\mathrm{thm{:}finite\text{-}saddle}\),
\[
 \frac1{\sqrt n}\le L_n(\mathcal E^{\mathrm{NI}},\bar p)
 \le\left\{\frac{n}{n-1}
 \left(\frac1{m_n}+\frac1{n-m_n}\right)\right\}^{1/2}. \tag{5}
\]
Since \(m_n/n\to\bar p\in(0,1)\), (5) is the claimed \(n^{-1/2}\) order. Both denominators are positive by admissibility; the prior is only a minimax certificate over fixed schedules, not superpopulation randomness. \(\square\)

statements.statement:
Fix \(\bar p\in(0,1)\) and consider \(n\in\mathcal N_{\bar p}\) along a diverging sequence. The conditional compression result in \(\mathrm{thm{:}orbit\text{-}fractional\text{-}cover\text{-}compression}\) already gives a quotient linear program that exactly computes \(\inf_\pi C_n(\pi)^2\), the squared optimized pairwise collision modulus, and a \(\sqrt{\kappa_n}\)-factor bracket for \(L_n(\mathcal E,\bar p)\) whenever an equivariant fractional diameter cover of congestion \(\kappa_n\) is supplied. These are automorphisms and fibers of the menu-induced sign experiment. The trivial-action construction in \(\mathrm{lem{:}universal\text{-}coarse\text{-}fractional\text{-}cover}\) gives congestion at most \(|\Omega_n|\), and hence
\[
 \inf_\pi U_n(\pi)
 \le |\Omega_n|^{1/2}\inf_\pi C_n(\pi),
\]
but this certificate can have exponential encoding length and its factor need not be uniform in \(n\). The residual problem is to identify and verify primitive budget and exposure-incidence conditions for natural graph-local menu sequences \(\mathcal E(G_n)\) that yield polynomial-encoding orbit tables, polynomially many orbit variables and constraints, and fractional diameter covers with \(\sup_n\kappa_n<\infty\). Here \(G_n\) constrains or organizes the menu and may certify useful actions or incidence bounds; every frontier effect is mediated through the resulting \(\mathcal E(G_n)\). More generally, establish or refute for such families a size-uniform reverse comparison
\[
 \inf_\pi U_n(\pi)\le K\inf_\pi C_n(\pi)
\]
for some finite \(K\) independent of \(n\). Determine separately whether a natural graph-local sequence can have identical mapping-wise labeled conflict-graph multisets but ambiguity frontiers separated by a nonvanishing amount. The unrestricted nonlocal witness in \(\mathrm{thm{:}persistent\text{-}nonrepresentability}\) does not answer that local question, and no natural graph-local separation is asserted here.

Fix \(\bar p\in[1/2,1)\), so \(2\in\mathcal N_{\bar p}\). For every \(\kappa\in\{0,-,+\}\),
\[
 V_2^\star(\{e^{(\kappa)}\},\bar p)=\frac56.
\]
Consequently,
\[
 \max_{\kappa\in\{0,-\}}V_2^\star(\{e^{(\kappa)}\},\bar p)
 =\max_{\kappa\in\{0,+\}}V_2^\star(\{e^{(\kappa)}\},\bar p)
 =\frac56.
\]
More generally, fix \(\bar p\in(0,1)\). For every \(B\ge1\) such that \(n=2B\in\mathcal N_{\bar p}\), and every \(\kappa\in\{0,-,+\}\),
\[
 V_{2B}^\star(\{\widetilde e^\kappa\},\bar p)=\frac56.
\]
Hence
\[
 \max_{\kappa\in\{0,-\}}V_{2B}^\star(\{\widetilde e^\kappa\},\bar p)
 =\max_{\kappa\in\{0,+\}}V_{2B}^\star(\{\widetilde e^\kappa\},\bar p)
 =\frac56.
\]
These identities hold for the full class of block-specific bounded response coordinates and arbitrary measurable estimators.
statements.proof_tex:
\textbf{Proof.}
For any one of the three two-unit mappings, write its four sign response coordinates, after a mapping-specific relabeling, as \((A,B,C,D)\). The relabeling may also reverse the two observed unit coordinates, which an estimator can undo. In all three cases the finite experiment is
\[
 t=\frac{B+D-A-C}{2},\qquad
 s_{10}=(A,C),\qquad s_{01}=(A,D). \tag{1}
\]
Indeed, for \(e^{(0)}\) this is the original coordinate order. For both \(e^{(-)}\) and \(e^{(+)}\), take \((A,B,C,D)=(c,d,a,b)\) and reverse observed-unit coordinates; for \(e^{(+)}\), also interchange the canonical names of assignments \(10\) and \(01\). The exposure tables in \(\mathrm{def{:}minimal\text{-}witness\text{-}mappings}\) verify (1).

Use the uniform design on \(\{10,01\}\) and the sign rule
\[
 \delta_{10}(A,C)=-\frac A2-\frac{2C}{3},
 \qquad
 \delta_{01}(A,D)=-\frac A2+\frac{2D}{3}. \tag{2}
\]
Its two errors are
\[
 \delta_{10}-t=-\frac{B+D}{2}-\frac C6,
 \qquad
 \delta_{01}-t=\frac{C-B}{2}+\frac D6. \tag{3}
\]
For the eight triples \((B,C,D)\in\{-1,1\}^3\), the average of the two squared expressions in (3) is \(25/36\), except at \((-1,-1,1)\) and \((1,1,-1)\), where it is \(1/36\). Thus the worst sign-schedule mean squared error is \(25/36\). The multilinear extension and \(\mathrm{lem{:}sign\text{-}reduction}\) extend this upper bound to every bounded response array.

For the matching lower bound, fix \(A=1\) and put a prior on \((B,C,D)\) with mass \(5/36\) on each of
\[
 (-1,-1,-1),\quad(-1,1,1),\quad(1,-1,-1),\quad(1,1,1),
\]
mass \(2/9\) on each of \((-1,1,-1)\) and \((1,-1,1)\), and zero elsewhere. These six masses sum to one. Direct summation gives
\[
 \mathbb E B=\mathbb E C=\mathbb E D=0,
 \quad
 \mathbb E(BC)=-\frac49,
 \quad
 \mathbb E(BD)=\frac49,
 \quad
 \mathbb E(CD)=\frac19. \tag{4}
\]
Consequently
\[
 \mathbb E(t\mid A,C)=-\frac A2-\frac{2C}{3},
 \qquad
 \mathbb E(t\mid A,D)=-\frac A2+\frac{2D}{3}. \tag{5}
\]
Also, with \(R=(B+D-C)/2\), equations (4) give
\[
 \mathbb E R^2
 =\frac14\{3+2\mathbb E(BD)-2\mathbb E(BC)-2\mathbb E(CD)\}
 =\frac{41}{36}. \tag{6}
\]
The squared conditional means of \(R\) given either \(C\) or \(D\) equal \(4/9\). Hence the posterior target variance, averaged over the observation, is
\[
 \frac{41}{36}-\frac49=\frac{25}{36} \tag{7}
\]
under either assignment. The posterior square-loss identity makes (7) a Bayes mean squared error lower bound under every design and every measurable estimator. Combining it with the upper bound proves
\[
 V_2^\star(\{e^{(\kappa)}\},\bar p)=\frac56
 \qquad(\kappa\in\{0,-,+\}). \tag{8}
\]

Now let \(n=2B\) and use \(\mathrm{def{:}persistent\text{-}witness}\). Admissibility implies \(\rho_B(\Omega_{2B})=\{10,01\}\): an assignment with the distinguished unit treated realizes \(10\), and one with it untreated realizes \(01\). Put half the design mass on one physical assignment of each selector type. Apply (2), after the same mapping-specific relabeling, to every block and average the block estimates. If block \(j\) has target \(t_j\) and error \(E_j\), then
\[
 \left(B^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^B E_j\right)^2
 \le B^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^B E_j^2. \tag{9}
\]
The sign calculation above bounds the design expectation of every term on the right by \(25/36\), even when the bounded response coordinates differ by block; sign reduction then covers arbitrary bounded coordinates. This proves the upper bound \(5/6\).

For the lower bound, draw one of the six prior atoms above and replicate that same atom in every block. Every physical assignment reveals replicated copies of exactly one canonical observation in (1), while the normalized block-average target equals the canonical target. Thus (7) applies under every physical assignment and therefore under every exact-budget design. The Bayes lower bound is again \(25/36\), proving
\[
 V_{2B}^\star(\{\widetilde e^\kappa\},\bar p)=\frac56.
\]
Taking the displayed maxima yields the two oracle-benchmark identities. All lower priors are supported on fixed bounded schedules, and the upper rules are measurable functions of the one realized assignment and outcome vector; no superpopulation sampling, assignment-level positivity, or locality condition is used. \(\square\)

statements.statement: Fix \(\bar p\in(0,1)\) and \(n\in\mathcal N_{\bar p}\). For the menu \(\mathcal E^{\mathrm{nl}}\), every probability vector \(\pi\) on \(\Omega_n\) satisfies \(C_n(\pi)=U_n(\pi)=2\), and \(V_n^\star(\mathcal E^{\mathrm{nl}},\bar p)=1\). Consequently equality holds in both sides of \(\mathrm{thm{:}collision\text{-}geometry\text{-}sandwich}\), so the universal factor \(1/2\) is sharp in both the lower and upper bounds.
statements.proof_tex:
\textbf{Proof.}
Every \(z\in\Omega_n\) differs from \(\mathbf 1_n\), because \(1\le m_n\le n-1\). Hence a sign schedule under \(e^{\mathrm{all}}\) is observed through its exposure-zero vector \(a=(a_i)_i\) at every feasible assignment, and its target is
\[
 t(a,b)=\frac1n\sum_{i\in V_n}(b_i-a_i), \tag{1}
\]
where \(b\) is its all-treated response vector. A sign schedule under \(e^{\mathrm c}\) has target zero.

Fix a feasible cell \((z,s)\). Among the \(e^{\mathrm{all}}\) schedules producing \(s\), take \(a=s\) and respectively \(b=\mathbf 1_n\) and \(b=-\mathbf 1_n\). Their target separation is two, so
\[
 d_n(z,s)\ge2. \tag{2}
\]
Conversely, the targets of all \(e^{\mathrm{all}}\) schedules in this fiber lie in
\[
 \left[-1-\frac1n\sum_i s_i, 1-\frac1n\sum_i s_i\right], \tag{3}
\]
an interval of length two containing zero. Adding any colliding constant-mapping schedule therefore does not enlarge the interval. Thus (2) is an equality for every feasible sign cell. It follows directly from the definition that \(U_n(\pi)=2\) for every probability vector \(\pi\).

The same two schedules collide at every feasible assignment and have target separation two, so \(C_n(\pi)\ge2\). Equation (3) shows that any two colliding schedules have target separation at most two, whence \(C_n(\pi)\le2\). Therefore \(C_n(\pi)=2\). Finally, \(\mathrm{prop{:}nonlocal\text{-}program\text{-}solution}\) gives \(V_n^\star(\mathcal E^{\mathrm{nl}},\bar p)=1\). Substitution into
\[
 \frac12\inf_\pi C_n(\pi)
 \le V_n^\star(\mathcal E^{\mathrm{nl}},\bar p)
 \le\frac12\inf_\pi U_n(\pi)
\]
makes both inequalities equalities. Hence neither universal factor \(1/2\) can be increased or decreased, respectively. Nonemptiness of \(\Omega_n\) and exclusion of the all-treated endpoint are guaranteed by \(n\in\mathcal N_{\bar p}\); no further support condition is used. \(\square\)

statements.statement:
Fix \(\bar p\in(0,1)\) and \(n\in\mathcal N_{\bar p}\), and write \(\mathfrak A_n=\mathcal B_n(\mathcal E)\). Suppose a finite group \(\Gamma_n\) acts on \(\Omega_n\) and on \(\mathfrak A_n\) such that, for every \(g\in\Gamma_n\) and \(z\in\Omega_n\), there is a bijection \(\phi_{g,z}:\mathcal S_n\to\mathcal S_n\) satisfying
\[
 t_{g\alpha}=t_\alpha,
 \qquad
 s_{g\alpha,gz}=\phi_{g,z}(s_{\alpha z})
 \quad\text{for every }\alpha\in\mathfrak A_n.
\]
Let \(O_1,\ldots,O_K\) be the assignment orbits and \(P_1,\ldots,P_R\) the orbits of unordered pairs of sign schedules. Choose \(p_r=\{\alpha_r,\beta_r\}\in P_r\), put \(\Delta_r=|t_{\alpha_r}-t_{\beta_r}|\), and define
\[
 a_{rj}=\frac{1}{|O_j|}\sum_{z\in O_j}
 \mathbf 1\{s_{\alpha_r z}=s_{\beta_r z}\}.
\]
Assume that there is a fractional diameter cover of congestion \(\kappa_n\ge1\): for one representative \(\alpha_h\) of every \(\Gamma_n\)-orbit in \(\mathfrak A_n\), there are unordered pairs \(p_{h\ell}=\{\beta_{h\ell},\gamma_{h\ell}\}\) and weights \(q_{h\ell}\ge0\) such that \(\sum_\ell q_{h\ell}\le\kappa_n\) and, for every \(z\in\Omega_n\),
\[
 d_n(z,s_{\alpha_h z})^2
 \le
 \sum_\ell q_{h\ell}
 |t_{\beta_{h\ell}}-t_{\gamma_{h\ell}}|^2
 \mathbf 1\{s_{\beta_{h\ell}z}=s_{\gamma_{h\ell}z}\}.
\]
For other schedules use the cover obtained by applying the same group element to every pair in the representative cover. Define
\[
 \lambda_n=\min_{x_1,\ldots,x_K,\lambda}
 \left\{\lambda:
 x_j\ge0,\ \sum_{j=1}^Kx_j=1,
 \Delta_r^2\sum_{j=1}^K a_{rj}x_j\le\lambda
 \text{ for }r=1,\ldots,R\right\}.
\]
Then
\[
 \inf_\pi C_n(\pi)=\sqrt{\lambda_n},
 \qquad
 \inf_\pi C_n(\pi)
 \le \inf_\pi U_n(\pi)
 \le \sqrt{\kappa_n}\inf_\pi C_n(\pi),
\]
and
\[
 \frac12\sqrt{\lambda_n}
 \le L_n(\mathcal E,\bar p)
 \le \frac12\sqrt{\kappa_n\lambda_n}.
\]
An optimizer \(x^\star\) lifts to the explicit invariant design assigning mass \(x_j^\star/|O_j|\) to every \(z\in O_j\); the observation-fiber midpoint rule and its multilinear extension have worst-case root mean squared error at most \(\sqrt{\kappa_n\lambda_n}/2\). Thus, if \(\sup_n\kappa_n<\infty\), the optimized collision moduli match in order. If the orbit tables and fractional cover have polynomial encoding length, the displayed certificate has \(K+1\) variables, \(R\) loss inequalities, \(K\) nonnegativity inequalities, and one simplex equality, and is polynomial-size whenever \(K\) and \(R\) are polynomial in \(n\). The actions here are automorphisms of the menu-induced sign experiment, not necessarily automorphisms of the ambient graph \(G_n\). In graph-local subclasses, \(G_n\) may constrain or organize a menu \(\mathcal E(G_n)\) and certify such actions or incidence bounds, but its effect on the frontier is mediated through the resulting menu. This criterion is sufficient, not exhaustive: mapping-wise conflict-graph multisets fail on the unrestricted class, while the analogous natural graph-local separation remains undecided.
statements.proof_tex:
\textbf{Proof.}
For an unordered pair \(p=\{\alpha,\beta\}\), define its squared collision loss under a design \(\pi\) by
\[
 F_p(\pi)=|t_\alpha-t_\beta|^2
 \sum_{z\in\Omega_n}\pi_z
 \mathbf 1\{s_{\alpha z}=s_{\beta z}\}. \tag{1}
\]
Then \(C_n(\pi)^2=\max_pF_p(\pi)\). The assumed target invariance and the bijectivity of \(\phi_{g,z}\) imply
\[
 F_{gp}(g\pi)=F_p(\pi), \tag{2}
\]
where \((g\pi)_{gz}=\pi_z\). Average any design over the finite group:
\[
 \bar\pi=|\Gamma_n|^{-1}\sum_{g\in\Gamma_n}g\pi. \tag{3}
\]
Because a maximum of linear functions is convex, (2) and (3) give
\[
 C_n(\bar\pi)^2
 \le |\Gamma_n|^{-1}\sum_g C_n(g\pi)^2
 =C_n(\pi)^2. \tag{4}
\]
Thus an optimizer may be taken invariant. Such a design is uniquely described by its orbit masses \(x_j\), assigning \(x_j/|O_j|\) to each member of \(O_j\). For the representative pair \(p_r\), equation (1) becomes
\[
 F_{p_r}(\pi)=\Delta_r^2\sum_{j=1}^K a_{rj}x_j. \tag{5}
\]
Equation (2) makes this value the same for every pair in \(P_r\). Minimizing the maximum of (5) over the simplex is exactly the displayed linear program. The simplex is compact and nonempty, so an optimizer exists, and
\[
 \inf_\pi C_n(\pi)^2=\lambda_n. \tag{6}
\]

For every design, every pair \(p=\{\alpha,\beta\}\), and every assignment where the pair collides, the fiber containing \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) has diameter at least \(|t_\alpha-t_\beta|\). Consequently
\[
 \sum_z\pi_zd_n(z,s_{\alpha z})^2\ge F_p(\pi),
\]
and maximizing first over schedules and then over pairs gives
\[
 U_n(\pi)\ge C_n(\pi). \tag{7}
\]

Let \(\pi\) now be invariant. The equivariant cover, applied to any schedule \(\alpha\), and then summed against \(\pi\), gives
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \sum_z\pi_zd_n(z,s_{\alpha z})^2
 &\le \sum_\ell q_{\alpha\ell}
 |t_{\beta_{\alpha\ell}}-t_{\gamma_{\alpha\ell}}|^2
 \sum_z\pi_z\mathbf 1\{s_{\beta_{\alpha\ell}z}=s_{\gamma_{\alpha\ell}z}\}\\
 &\le \left(\sum_\ell q_{\alpha\ell}\right)C_n(\pi)^2
 \le\kappa_n C_n(\pi)^2. \tag{8}
 \end{aligned}
\]
The first inequality for an orbit translate is valid because the action carries fibers bijectively, preserves targets, and \(\pi\) is invariant. Maximizing (8) over \(\alpha\) yields \(U_n(\pi)\le\sqrt{\kappa_n}C_n(\pi)\). Apply this to the invariant optimizer from (6), and combine it with (7), to obtain
\[
 \inf_\pi C_n(\pi)
 \le\inf_\pi U_n(\pi)
 \le\sqrt{\kappa_n}\inf_\pi C_n(\pi). \tag{9}
\]

By \(\mathrm{thm{:}finite\text{-}saddle}\), \(L_n(\mathcal E,\bar p)=V_n^\star(\mathcal E,\bar p)\). Applying \(\mathrm{thm{:}collision\text{-}geometry\text{-}sandwich}\), (6), and (9) gives
\[
 \frac12\sqrt{\lambda_n}
 \le L_n(\mathcal E,\bar p)
 \le\frac12\sqrt{\kappa_n\lambda_n}. \tag{10}
\]
The optimizer \(x^\star\) produces exactly the invariant design stated in the theorem. The observation-fiber midpoint rule used in the sandwich theorem, followed by \(\mathrm{def{:}multilinear\text{-}extension}\), has worst-case root mean squared error at most \(U_n(\pi^\star)/2\), which is at most the right side of (10).

If \(\sup_n\kappa_n<\infty\), (9) is a size-uniform constant-factor comparison. The displayed linear program has the asserted \(K+1\) variables, \(R\) pair-orbit inequalities, \(K\) nonnegativity inequalities, and one simplex equality; hence polynomially bounded \(K,R\) and polynomially encoded coefficients and cover data give a polynomial-size certificate. The action was assumed only on the menu-induced sign experiment. Nothing in (1)--(10) requires it to arise from \(G_n\). If a graph-local construction uses \(G_n\) to specify \(\mathcal E(G_n)\) or certify the action and cover, its mathematical effect enters through those menu-experiment objects. Finally, \(\mathrm{thm{:}persistent\text{-}nonrepresentability}\) and \(\mathrm{prop{:}nonlocal\text{-}collision\text{-}sharpness}\) establish only the stated unrestricted limitations and sharpness; they do not turn this sufficient conditional criterion into an exhaustive characterization. No assignment-level positivity beyond the nonempty exact-budget support, rank condition, or unmentioned locality condition is used. \(\square\)

statements.statement:
Fix \(\bar p\in(0,1)\) and \(n\in\mathcal N_{\bar p}\). For the trivial group actions on \(\Omega_n\) and \(\mathcal B_n(\mathcal E)\), which are actions on the menu-induced sign experiment, the fractional-diameter-cover hypothesis of \(\mathrm{thm{:}orbit\text{-}fractional\text{-}cover\text{-}compression}\) holds with congestion at most \(|\Omega_n|\). Consequently,
\[
 \inf_\pi U_n(\pi)
 \le |\Omega_n|^{1/2}\inf_\pi C_n(\pi),
\]
and
\[
 \frac12\inf_\pi C_n(\pi)
 \le L_n(\mathcal E,\bar p)
 \le \frac12|\Omega_n|^{1/2}\inf_\pi C_n(\pi).
\]
statements.proof_tex:
\textbf{Proof.}
Take both group actions to be trivial. Then every sign schedule is its own orbit representative. Fix such a schedule \(\alpha\). For each \(z\in\Omega_n\) with \(d_n(z,s_{\alpha z})>0\), finiteness of \(\mathcal B_n(\mathcal E)\) supplies schedules \(\beta_z,\gamma_z\) in the fiber \(\{\eta:s_{\eta z}=s_{\alpha z}\}\) attaining its maximum and minimum target. Put weight one on the unordered pair \(\{\beta_z,\gamma_z\}\). Assign no pair when the diameter is zero. There are at most \(|\Omega_n|\) positive weights, so their sum is at most \(|\Omega_n|\).

At any fixed \(z_0\), the term indexed by \(z_0\), when present, satisfies
\[
 |t_{\beta_{z_0}}-t_{\gamma_{z_0}}|^2
 \mathbf 1\{s_{\beta_{z_0}z_0}=s_{\gamma_{z_0}z_0}\}
 =d_n(z_0,s_{\alpha z_0})^2. \tag{1}
\]
All other terms are nonnegative. If the left side diameter is zero, the required inequality is automatic. Thus these pairs and weights satisfy the fractional-diameter-cover condition with congestion at most \(|\Omega_n|\). Applying \(\mathrm{thm{:}orbit\text{-}fractional\text{-}cover\text{-}compression}\) with \(\kappa_n=|\Omega_n|\) gives
\[
 \inf_\pi U_n(\pi)
 \le |\Omega_n|^{1/2}\inf_\pi C_n(\pi)
\]
and the two displayed bounds for \(L_n(\mathcal E,\bar p)\). The construction uses only finiteness and nonemptiness of the exact-budget assignment set and sign-schedule set; it requires no assignment-level positivity, rank, graph action, or locality. \(\square\)

sampling_model.design: Fix \(\bar p\in(0,1)\) and \(n\in\mathcal N_{\bar p}\). One assignment \(Z\sim\Theta\) is drawn, where the experimenter chooses any \(\Theta\in\mathcal D_n(\bar p)\).
sampling_model.units: At each \(n\in\mathcal N_{\bar p}\), the population \(V_n\), graph \(G_n\), and potential-outcome table \(y\) are fixed; there is no superpopulation sampling.
sampling_model.treatment: Binary treatment with exact treated count \(m_n=\lfloor\bar p n\rfloor\), where admissibility guarantees \(1\le m_n\le n-1\).
sampling_model.overlap: Neither endpoint assignment is feasible; endpoint exposure values are learned only when a candidate mapping makes them coincide with exposures on \(\Omega_n\).
sampling_model.nuisance_estimation: The latent mapping is not observed or estimated; the estimator may use \(G_n,\mathcal E,\bar p,Z,Y^{\mathrm{obs}}\).
sampling_model.randomness: Assignment under \(\Theta\) is the only physical randomness; sign randomization appears only in the proof of the lossless finite reduction.

estimand_functional: \(V_n^\star(\mathcal E,\bar p)=L_n(\mathcal E,\bar p)=\sqrt{\operatorname{val}(\mathsf P_n)}=\sqrt{\operatorname{val}(\mathsf Q_n)}\text{ attained by }(\Theta_n^\star,\widehat\theta_n^\star),\quad n\in\mathcal N_{\bar p}\)

tldr: For fixed \(\bar p\in(0,1)\), a one-shot exact-budget experiment at \(n\in\mathcal N_{\bar p}\) must estimate the all-treated-versus-all-control effect when a fixed bounded potential-outcome table obeys one unknown member of a finite exposure-mapping menu. Sign-valued exposure responses yield an exact finite decision reduction, and multilinear extension recovers a lossless rule for arbitrary bounded outcomes and unrestricted estimators. A finite second-order cone primal and least-favourable-prior dual compute the minimax root mean squared error and recover an attaining design and rule. At \(\bar p=1/2\), two cardinality-two menu sequences on every even population size have the same multisets of labeled mapping-wise conflict graphs but exact risks \(1\) and \(5/4\), so cross-model observation cells remain essential asymptotically. A primitive collision-modulus sandwich gives directly evaluable necessary and sufficient conditions on opposite sides of remediability, while matching structural compression remains open.

project_justification.gap: Faridani and Niehaus study the same global average treatment effect and jointly derive minimax rates over designs and linear estimators under spillovers decaying in a known generalized distance. Other work characterizes one known ANI model, tests nested exposure specifications, or optimizes a correctly specified linear spillover model. Schröder, Oprescu, Feuerriegel, and Kallus derive sharp sensitivity and partial-identification bounds under exposure-mapping misspecification for both experimental and observational data, taking the assignment regime as fixed or externally given; they neither choose an exact-treated-count design nor solve an unrestricted design--estimator minimax saddle over a latent finite exposure menu. No comparator gives a finite exact saddle over arbitrary estimators and unrestricted bounded response tables for that latent union.
project_justification.niche: Finite exposure ranges make each candidate model finite-dimensional, but real response coordinates and arbitrary estimators initially leave an infinite decision problem. The sign-reduction theorem exposes a lossless finite experiment whose observation cells preserve cross-model collisions.
project_justification.fill: The finite primal and least-favourable-prior dual compute the exact minimax risk at each \(n\in\mathcal N_{\bar p}\) and recover an attaining design and lossless multilinear representative. The collision-geometry sandwich exposes primitive lower and upper certificates, and at \(\bar p=1/2\) the persistent even-population witness proves that the required information is strictly richer than a multiset of mapping-wise conflict graphs.

related_work: Faridani and Niehaus (2024, revised January 2026) study the same all-treated-versus-none global average treatment effect and jointly derive minimax rates over experimental designs and linear estimators when spillovers decay with a known generalized distance. That comparison is closer than known-operator variance optimization, but it does not cover an unknown member of a finite exposure menu, unrestricted bounded exposure-response tables, arbitrary nonlinear estimators, or the exact finite cross-model observation-cell saddle; the multilinear rule here is recovered losslessly from the unrestricted minimax problem rather than assumed as a linear or Riesz class. Kandiros, Harshaw, and Sävje (2026), Section 2.3, Proposition 2.2; restated and proved in Appendix A.5, show that for an interference network \(G\), a fixed contrastive effect \(\tau\), and \(q\ge2\), there exists a function \(f_q\) on labeled graphs such that \(R(G,\tau,q)=f_q(H)\) for the single known model's conflict graph \(H\). Appendix A.5 reproduces the main-body Proposition 2.2 under its original number and supplies its proof; Proposition A.4 is a separate outcome-restriction result. At \(\bar p=1/2\), the persistent even-population construction preserves the full multiset of mapping-wise graphs but keeps risks \(1\) and \(5/4\) under a latent cardinality-two union on the exact-treated-count slice. Gao, Harshaw, Sävje, and Wang (2026), Theorem 3.1 in Section 3.3, proves minimax testing error one for a null exposure model against a nontrivially separated nested alternative; it does not study squared-error estimation of the global effect and supplies neither an attaining estimator nor a two-sided design frontier. Schröder, Oprescu, Feuerriegel, and Kallus (2026) derive sharp sensitivity and partial-identification bounds under exposure-mapping misspecification for both experimental and observational data, taking the assignment regime as fixed or externally given; they neither choose an exact-treated-count design nor solve an unrestricted design--estimator minimax saddle over a latent finite exposure menu. Borusyak, Hull, and Munro (2026) jointly optimize design and recentered instrumental-variables analysis for one correctly specified linear spillover operator. Viviano (2026 revision) optimizes network design under known local interference and names alternative exposure mappings as an open design issue. Kandiros, Pipis, Daskalakis, and Harshaw (2024) construct a conflict-graph design for a prespecified effect under a known neighborhood model. Basse and Airoldi (2018) provide the arbitrary-interference negative benchmark. Aronow and Samii (2017) provide the standard single exposure-mapping response model.
honest_scope: For fixed \(\bar p\in(0,1)\), every finite program and asymptotic sequence is indexed by \(n\in\mathcal N_{\bar p}\). The exact finite programs can be exponentially large in the number of exposure-response coordinates and assignments; polynomial-time computation and compressed graph summaries remain open. The menu is finite with fixed cardinality, response arrays are arbitrary in \([-1,1]\), assignments obey one exact treated-count budget, and the estimator observes one realization. No graph locality, smoothness, linear response, common representer, endpoint support, or estimator restriction is imposed. The collision sandwich supplies one sufficient and one necessary primitive condition for each asymptotic regime; equality of the optimized moduli and an exhaustive natural-menu classification remain open. At \(\bar p=1/2\), the persistent separation uses an engineered nonlocal common selector. Under the singleton no-interference mapping, complete randomization and difference in means recover the classical \(n^{-1/2}\) rate along admissible indices.
